title: 2 Kings 2:13–22
context: Elisha takes up Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, goes back to the bank of the Jordan, and strikes the waters, saying, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” When he has struck the waters, they are divided apart, and he goes over. The sons of the prophets who were at Jericho, facing him, say, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.” They come to meet him and bow to the ground, then ask leave to send fifty strong men to seek his master, “Perhaps the LORD’s Spirit has taken him up, and put him on some mountain or into some valley.” Elisha says, “Don’t send them.” They urge him until he is ashamed, and he says, “Send them.” They search for three days and do not find him. When they come back to him at Jericho, he says, “Didn’t I tell you, ‘Don’t go’?” The men of the city then tell him that the situation of the city is pleasant, but the water is bad and the land is barren. He asks for a new jar with salt in it, goes out to the spring, throws the salt in, and says, “The LORD says, ‘I have healed these waters. There shall not be from there any more death or barren wasteland.’ ” The waters were healed to this day, according to Elisha’s word. Both traditions read the mantle, the crossing, and the company’s confession as the public sign that Elisha now stands in the work he had asked to receive. The search shows that the sons of the prophets have not yet grasped the taking up as he has. The healing of the water is reported as the LORD’s word through Elisha, without turning the jar or the salt into a type.

verses.text: He also took up Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, and went back and stood by the bank of the Jordan.
verses.arminianNotes:
He also took up Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, and went back and stood by the bank of the Jordan. The mantle is the one already used at the crossing, now fallen and taken up, and Elisha returns to the river alone.

Arminian readers hear a real act of taking up what was left. He does not wait at the far side; he goes back to the bank with the mantle in hand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the fallen mantle in view. It fell from Elijah; Elisha takes it up and stands again by the Jordan.

Both traditions take the verse as the first movement after the taking up, the sign still in his hands, before he speaks or strikes the water.

verses.text: He took Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, and struck the waters, and said, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” When he also had struck the waters, they were divided apart, and Elisha went over.
verses.arminianNotes:
He took Elijah’s mantle that fell from him, and struck the waters, and said, “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” When he also had struck the waters, they were divided apart, and Elisha went over. The question is not a doubt left unanswered; the waters divide, and he crosses.

Arminian readers hear a real cry and a real answer in the event. He asks where the LORD, the God of Elijah, is, and the same river yields to him as it had to Elijah.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the mantle, the blow, the question, and the dividing belong together. “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” is spoken as he strikes, and Elisha goes over.

Both traditions read the crossing as the LORD’s confirmation of the work now in Elisha’s hands, without a party contrast over prophetic authority.

verses.text: When the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho facing him saw him, they said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.” They came to meet him, and bowed themselves to the ground before him.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the sons of the prophets who were at Jericho facing him saw him, they said, “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.” They came to meet him, and bowed themselves to the ground before him. The watchers from verse 7 now name what they see.

Arminian readers hear a confession from the company, not a coronation they invent. They see him, they say that Elijah’s spirit rests on him, and they bow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take their word as recognition of what the crossing has shown: “The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha.”

Both traditions receive that sentence as the company’s own judgment, matching the request of verse 9 as far as the narrative has now displayed it.

verses.text: They said to him, “See now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. Perhaps the LORD’s Spirit has taken him up, and put him on some mountain or into some valley.” He said, “Don’t send them.”
verses.arminianNotes:
They said, “See now, there are with your servants fifty strong men. Please let them go and seek your master. Perhaps the LORD’s Spirit has taken him up, and put him on some mountain or into some valley.” He said, “Don’t send them.” Their “Perhaps” still looks for Elijah on the land.

Arminian readers hear a sincere but incomplete reading of what has happened. They speak of the LORD’s Spirit taking him up, yet they think of a mountain or a valley, and Elisha tells them not to send.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the refusal: “Don’t send them.” Elisha does not share their “Perhaps”. He has seen the taking up, and he will not have a search begun.

Both traditions leave the gap in view. The company honors him, and still has not grasped what he saw.

verses.text: When they urged him until he was ashamed, he said, “Send them.” Therefore they sent fifty men; and they searched for three days, but didn’t find him.
verses.arminianNotes:
When they urged him until he was ashamed, he said, “Send them.” Therefore they sent fifty men; and they searched for three days, but didn’t find him. He yields to their urging, and the search fails.

Arminian readers hear a reluctant permission, not a change of mind about the fact. He is ashamed under their pressure, he lets them go, and three days find nothing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the result next to the permission. “Send them.” is spoken, fifty go, and they do not find him.

Both traditions take the failed search as confirmation of the taking up already told, not as a new question about whether Elijah still walks the hills.

verses.text: They came back to him while he stayed at Jericho; and he said to them, “Didn’t I tell you, ‘Don’t go’?”
verses.arminianNotes:
They came back to him while he stayed at Jericho; and he said to them, “Didn’t I tell you, ‘Don’t go’?” He had said not to send them; they have now learned why.

Arminian readers hear a plain reminder, not a taunt. He had told them, and the empty search has borne him out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same short word: “Didn’t I tell you, ‘Don’t go’?” The company returns to Jericho, and to the man who had refused the search at first.

Both traditions close this part of the unit on that reminder, and turn with the narrative to the city’s water.

verses.text: The men of the city said to Elisha, “Behold, please, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord sees; but the water is bad, and the land is barren.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The men of the city said to Elisha, “Behold, please, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord sees; but the water is bad, and the land is barren.” Jericho is fair in site and sick in its water and land.

Arminian readers hear a straightforward appeal. They do not ask for a sign against a rival; they name a pleasant city, bad water, and barren land.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the problem as they state it. The water is bad, and the land is barren, in a place otherwise pleasant.

Both traditions read the verse as the occasion of the healing that follows, without turning Jericho’s site into a symbol beyond the need they name.

verses.text: He said, “Bring me a new jar, and put salt in it.” Then they brought it to him.
verses.arminianNotes:
He said, “Bring me a new jar, and put salt in it.” Then they brought it to him. The means he asks for are a new jar and salt; the men do as he says.

Arminian readers hear a simple instruction, not a rite whose parts must be decoded in advance. A new jar, with salt in it, is what he requests, and they bring it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse to load the jar and the salt with a typology the verse does not state. He asks, and they bring it to him.

Both traditions wait for the act at the spring. The objects are given as the prophet names them, nothing more in this line.

verses.text: He went out to the spring of the waters, and threw salt into it, and said, “The LORD says, ‘I have healed these waters. There shall not be from there any more death or barren wasteland.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
He went out to the spring of the waters, and threw salt into it, and said, “The LORD says, ‘I have healed these waters. There shall not be from there any more death or barren wasteland.’ ” The healing is the LORD’s word, spoken as the salt is thrown into the spring.

Arminian readers hear a real promise about these waters. Death and barren wasteland are not to come from there any more, because the LORD says he has healed them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the sentence is the LORD’s: “I have healed these waters.” The salt is used, and the word does the work the verse names.

Both traditions keep the saying intact and decline to turn the gesture into a type. The result is told in the next verse.

verses.text: So the waters were healed to this day, according to Elisha’s word which he spoke.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the waters were healed to this day, according to Elisha’s word which he spoke.” The healing holds, the narrator says, to this day, and it is according to the word Elisha spoke.

Arminian readers hear a fulfilled word in the city’s water, lasting as the book records it. What he spoke in the LORD’s name has been done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the close as confirmation: the waters were healed to this day, according to Elisha’s word.

Both traditions end the unit on that lasting healing, the public work of the prophet who has now crossed the Jordan in Elijah’s mantle.
